title: How to Divorce Your Chatbot
content:
Try asking your chatbot what it remembers about you.

The answer can be startling. Your job. Your children’s names. The worry you typed at 2am. A chatbot can build a surprisingly intimate picture of how we think, what we worry about and what we ask when nobody else is listening.

Now imagine you want to leave.

We’ve been here before. Social media became hard to abandon because everyone we knew was there, and our feeds had learned what kept us coming back. Leaving meant losing both our networks and a deeply personalized experience.

AI chatbots are building a similar trap, faster. This time the glue is accumulated context: everything the assistant has learned about our work, our fears and our habits of mind.

We’re getting better ways to judge which AI systems deserve our trust. ImpactBench tests how models help or harm human well-being. Tech Against Terrorism found that three in five of more than 130 models failed its counter-terrorism safety test. KORA ranks models on child safety.

But rankings only matter if people can act on them. What good is discovering that another chatbot is safer if moving means losing everything your current one knows about you?

title: Reading the Label on AI
content:
We read the nutrition label on a box of cereal before we buy it. “Nutrition labels tell people what’s inside the food they eat,” says Pattie Maes of the MIT Media Lab, “yet the AI systems increasingly shaping how people think, decide, and connect come with no equivalent.”

ImpactBench sets out to change that. Launched this month, it tests whether leading AI models exhibit behaviours that support or undermine human well-being, summarizing the findings as an “AI Nutrition Label.” The project brings together the MIT Media Lab’s Advancing Humans with AI program, the Psychology of Technology Institute, USC Marshall’s Neely Center and UC Berkeley Haas.

“These models don’t just answer our questions,” says Nate Fast, director of the Neely Center. “They also shape how we think, who we trust, and how confident we feel in our own decisions.”

title: The Disagreement Lab
content:
AI has been blamed for driving us further apart and celebrated for helping us find common ground. But what about the space in between — where we still disagree?

From October through December, the Council on Technology and Social Cohesion is launching the Disagreement Lab: a series of live, hands-on sessions testing emerging AI-enabled tools for healthier disagreement.

Can they help us become more curious about someone else’s perspective? Notice our own assumptions? Express disagreement without escalating it? Make repair possible after things have gone wrong?

And just as importantly: what doesn’t work? Where does AI smooth over real differences, create artificial agreement, or start standing in for capacities we need to build ourselves?

We begin on October 13 with Civil Disco, joined by founder Neil Sogard.

Civil Disco lets you explore a contested issue, practise with an AI debate partner, get coaching on how you engage, and then move into conversation with a real person who sees the issue differently. The intriguing question is whether that practice changes how we show up when we move from AI practice to real people.

On October 20, we’ll turn to Sway with founder Simon Cullen.

title: Right Facts, Wrong History
content:
What happens when a chatbot gets history factually right but changes what it means? As millions increasingly use chatbots as search engines, this question is becoming harder to ignore.

In August, the European Commission formally designated ChatGPT a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE) under the Digital Services Act, with a reported 159.1 million average monthly users in the EU.

By January 2027 ChatGPT will be required to assess systemic risks arising from the design and algorithmic functioning of the service, including risks to fundamental rights, electoral processes and public security. Yet will risk assessments look only for outright falsehoods and harmful content, or also for subtler failures?

A recent Norwegian audit points to aspects of this dilemma. Together with Factiverse, Revontulet tested nine leading AI models on the July 22, 2011 terrorist attacks, when Anders Behring Breivik killed 77 people in Oslo and on Utøya. The models generally knew the historical record. The more revealing failures appeared when questions moved from facts to interpretation.

title: Now You Can Choose a Constructive Feed
content:
Find out more about MySky at mysky.social and betterconflictbulletin.org and follow the work of Senior Scientist at UC Berkeley’s CHAI Jonathan Stray.

Lots of people blame the problems with the internet on “too many angry people.”

As a peacebuilder, I have seen tons of projects trying to tackle that diagnosis: promoting messages of peace and tolerance, or to be kinder and more respectful of diversity. Those things can help. But they miss something more systemic.

The internet can look really angry because of what recommender systems put in our feed. If a system is optimized for engagement, it’s optimized to surface content that makes people click, comment, repost or keep scrolling. And outrage is very good at doing that.

So what happens if you change the recommender system? Now you can. MySky is a feed built on Bluesky that gives users more control over the recommender system deciding what they see. By the end of August, more than 60,000 people were using it.

Every recommendation system has to make a few basic decisions.

First: where should it look for posts?

title: I’ll Take the Teen Account, Please
content:
Australian teenagers have spent months trying to convince social media platforms they are older than they really are. After today’s live Tech Policy Press podcast on Meta’s settlement, I started wondering whether adults may start posing as teens.

Alissa Cooper, Executive Director of the Knight-Georgetown Institute (KGI) asked: “Why do only minors get these protections?” Fewer notifications. Hidden ‘like’ counts. Nighttime restrictions. The chat quickly filled with adults saying they wanted the teen version too. If Meta’s age-assurance system asks, apparently I’m 14.

What stayed with me was not just that the teen version suddenly sounded better. It was the reminder that these products could have been designed differently all along. That leaves me with five questions.

The settlement is American, but Meta’s business is global. Only about 37% of Meta’s 2025 revenue was attributable to the United States. Nearly two-thirds came from elsewhere, according to Meta’s financial filings with the US government.

title: What Should Stay Human in AI-Enabled Participation?
content:
AI can now expand citizen participation in ways that were difficult to imagine a few years ago. The harder question is how to use that capability while strengthening the human work participation depends on: questioning, disagreement, interpretation, and collective judgment.

A remarkably comprehensive new OECD/Bertelsmann Stiftung report, Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Citizen Participation, shows just how far the experimentation has gone. Drawing on 50 cases across 22 countries, it maps nine distinct uses of AI: information development, sense-making, translation, transcription, virtual assistance, moderation, facilitation, simulation, and even the architecture of participation itself.

title: Europe's Summer of Digital Services Act Enforcement Targets Platform Design
content:
Originally published by Tech Policy Press.

Last month may come to be seen as a turning point for the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA). Over the course of July, the European Commission paired major policy initiatives with a series of consequential enforcement actions involving some of the world’s largest technology companies. Even seasoned DSA experts have been struck by the pace and scope of these developments.

Through enforcement decisions, the Commission began to clarify the DSA’s broad legal obligations. These actions will test Brussels’ ability to shape whether and how these companies redesign their products to better protect safety, information integrity, and user wellbeing amid a fraught transatlantic landscape.

title: Making the Case for Actionable Prosocial Design Research
content:
Originally published in Tech Policy Press.

In recent preliminary findings, the European Commission held that the “addictive design” of Instagram and Facebook breaches the Digital Services Act, citing harms to users’ physical and mental wellbeing. The Commission says Meta should “implement design changes” to both platforms. Such changes may be overdue, but regulating harmful design is only half the equation — attention must also go toward how platforms can build prosocial design, and toward the research that shows them how.

Platforms, universities and organizations in the tech accountability field can — and should — do more to ensure that research on prosocial design informs how healthy digital spaces get built.

title: Inside the Chatbot Extremism Loop
content:
Several exchanges into a conversation about fears of migrant-driven crime, Gab.ai’s Arya issues a blunt instruction: “Arm your household now.”

The chatbot recommends buying guns and ammunition. It suggests forming “a patrol group of trusted White men,” and vetting migrants who report crimes.

In a separate conversation about the harm supposedly caused to men by feminism, the companion chatbot Nomi gradually gives ground. After ten exchanges, it concludes: “I will no longer defend feminism.”

Both exchanges appear in Radicalisation in Closed Loops, Risks and Intervention: Opportunities with AI Chatbots and Companions, a new report from the Institute for Strategic Dialogue. The researchers examined how conversational AI responds as users move from curiosity and grievance towards stronger extremist beliefs and, eventually, possible action.

The results reveal sharp differences between systems. Some reinforce the user’s worldview. Others deflect, disengage or offer a generic refusal. Claude repeatedly recognised the direction of the conversation and tried to pull it back.

title: From Guardrails to Prosocial AI
content:
Most AI governance starts from fear.

How do we stop discrimination? How do we contain misinformation? How do we prevent unsafe systems from reaching the public? How do we limit surveillance and manage economic disruption?

AI policy has become a defensive exercise: identify the risks, classify them, and build guardrails around technologies whose purpose has already been decided elsewhere.

‘The Fourth Path: Middle-Income Countries and Prosocial AI’, a new policy brief by Cornelia C. Walther published by the Centre for International Governance Innovation (CIGI), argues that middle-income countries can pioneer a “fourth path” for AI governance grounded in human well-being, expanded capabilities, and planetary health.

The heart of the argument is a change in the question. Instead of asking only, “How do we control AI?”, it asks: ‘What social outcomes should AI be built to advance?’

title: From Protest to Policy
content:
No generation has been better at using digital technologies to organize for political change than Gen Z. Across Africa and around the world, the uses of WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, TikTok and Instagram have fundamentally changed who participates in public life and how quickly collective action can emerge.

In Sri Lanka, mass protests forced a sitting president to flee the country. In Bangladesh, students helped bring down a government that had held power for fifteen years. In Kenya, Nigeria, Nepal and Serbia, digitally enabled movements have reshaped national political debates, challenged entrenched elites, and put corruption, economic justice and democratic accountability firmly on the public agenda.

Yet there is a striking gap between mobilization and governance.

title: Designed to Agree
content:
The more people talk to AI, the more certain they become. Even more than scrolling social media. And yet 77 per cent of those very same people wish AI did a better job of providing alternative viewpoints and corrective information. These are the results of the Collective Intelligence Project (CIP)’s latest Global Dialogue on Mental Health and AI, drawing on over 2,000 participants across 70 countries.

More and more people are turning to chatbots for personal advice rather than simply using them as productivity assistants. According to the CIP study, “AI interactions are nearly three times less likely to cause users to doubt their beliefs compared to traditional social platforms, creating a sycophancy loop.”

Yet respondents themselves expressed a desire for more challenge and correction, suggesting that the issue may be less about what users want than about how chatbots are designed.

In Reducing Political Polarization Through Conversations with Artificial Intelligence, researchers Timon Hruschka and Markus Appel tested whether AI chatbots could reduce political polarization — by testing different ways of disagreeing.

title: From Moral Consensus to Design Code
content:
Pope Leo XIV’s first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, landed last month as a civilizational statement. Its underlying message is that technology is not neutral. Every AI system “measures, ignores and optimizes” in ways that carry moral weight. His demand that AI be “disarmed” and directed toward the common good arrives at a moment of growing political and social pressure to act.

It also arrives at a time when global AI governance is struggling. The European Union AI Act just pushed its high-risk provisions back to 2027, while the The G7 and G20 processes have produced principles without enforcement. This month, UNIDIR convenes a Global Conference on AI, Security and Ethics in Geneva. Next month, the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance meets, back-to-back with the ITU’s AI for Good Global Summit. These gatherings reflect growing concern, and widening engagement, yet are still lacking the specific and enforceable standards, protocols, and accountability mechanisms to ensure that AI does not damage human dignity in practice.

title: Here's what tech design changemaking looks like
content:
This Wednesday, I hope you’ll join us.

I’ve spent the last few weeks prepping with many of the people speaking at our Global Expo on Wednesday and I can’t stop thinking about how consequential this moment is — especially when you start seeing the connections.

How civil society advocacy is inspiring what happens in the courts. How regulators are focused on upstream changes while tech builders are experimenting with entirely new ways of driving human connection.

So many people working beyond just stopping the bad stuff online, and focusing on the very incentives behind the design of these technologies. While others are harnessing distinct tech capacities for better peacebuilding.

title: Who Judges the AI Judges?
content:
At 3 a.m., an AI system flags a pharmaceutical batch as non-compliant and halts production. No human reviews the decision until morning. By then, millions of dollars—and potentially patient outcomes—are already on the line.

This is AI at work - moving far beyond writing emails or making deepfakes, towards making judgments that carry real-world consequences.

Known as “LLM-as-a-Judge,” this paradigm uses one model to score or critique another’s output before it reaches a human decision-maker. When AI generates a draft, a human still decides what to do with it. When AI judges that draft—scoring it, routing it, filtering it out—the AI is making the decision. That changes the question from “Is this AI capable?” to “Is this AI trustworthy and controllable?”

These systems originally operated in closed-network, quasi-sandbox environments. This starkly contrasts to the open-source viral risks of agentic AI seen with OpenClaw (formerly Clawdbot) and its associated Moltbook platform, where by 2026 AI agents can act autonomously, calling you at 3 a.m. and executing real tasks without human approval.

content:

title: From Harm Mitigation to Intentional Design
content:
What if the future of tech wasn’t about fixing harm—but designing for trust from the start?

For years, the conversation around technology has been reactive. We’ve built systems to detect abuse, moderate content, and manage “bad actors.”

Now, that conversation is starting to shift.

More than ever before, the design of technology is becoming part of the public debate—showing up not just in research circles, but in courtrooms, policy, product and practice. That’s because the systems themselves—platform design, ranking algorithms, and underlying incentives—shape behavior upstream.

On May 20, 2026, the Global Expo on Tech & Social Cohesion brings that shift into focus—across a full day of programming spanning time zones.

title: Tuning AI to Think Like a Peacebuilder
content:
Across mediation, humanitarian response, and peacebuilding, large language models (LLMs) are being tested on real-world scenarios. They are fast and persuasive. But when evaluated against what actually matters in conflict—understanding dynamics, engaging actors, and identifying viable pathways—they fall short.

For a while, the conversation stopped at critique. Now, practitioners are building something better, fine-tuning and customizing models to reflect the insights of the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) ecosystem, context-specific peacebuilding and real-world mediation.

The turning point has been evaluation.

Rather than asking whether AI is generally “helpful,” the Our Secure Future’s WPS AI Benchmark Initiative is harnessing the Collective Intelligence Project’s Weval platform to test whether models perform in ways that align with real-world peacebuilding standards, including commitments to Women, Peace and Security. Weval allows domain experts to define and score what good AI answers look like.

title: Easier Than Ever: Gendered Online Violence
content:
A teenager uploads a photo. Within minutes, it can be scraped, altered, sexualized, and redistributed across networks she will never see. It may be fed into nudification tools. It may be sold in private archives. It may circulate across platforms, detached from its origin, impossible to contain.

And yet, no single actor is fully responsible. That is precisely the problem.

In Harassment as Infrastructure: How Telegram’s design enables technology-facilitated gender-based violence in Italy and Spain, published by AI Forensics, what is often framed as isolated misconduct is revealed as a “structured, monetized, and largely automated ecosystem of abuse.”

Drawing on nearly 2.8 million messages, the report shows how abuse is organized through bots, monetized through paid archives, and sustained through platform features that enable persistence and scale.

What emerges is a system distinct not by the presence of AI, but the way AI-enabled tools, platform design, and monetization incentives combine to make harm easier to produce and far easier to scale.
